common_name: Hope Diamond Daylily (Classic Near-White Dwarf Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Hope Diamond is a compact 1968-introduced diploid, among the earlier hybrids bred toward a true near-white daylily.

directions: Hope Diamond is a dwarf, dormant-foliage daylily introduced in 1968, bearing small near-white self flowers with only a faint cream cast, an early milestone in the long breeding push toward a genuinely white daylily. Scapes stand little more than a foot tall and open an early-to-midseason flush with some rebloom, making it a tidy front-of-border or rock-garden choice rather than a back-of-bed specimen. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Lavender Dew Daylily (Ruffled Lavender Blend with Lime-Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Lavender Dew is a 1976 introduction with evergreen foliage and an extended midseason bloom.

directions: Lavender Dew bears large, ruffled-edge lavender-blend flowers over a cool lime-green throat, carried on scapes around two feet tall. This diploid, evergreen cultivar was introduced in 1976, flowering over an extended midseason period rather than a single short flush, and has a long reputation among growers for good rust resistance. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain heavy bloom.

common_name: Chicago Brave Daylily (Dark Red Self with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Chicago Brave is a 1976 introduction that reblooms through summer and earned an American Hemerocallis Society Honorable Mention.

directions: Chicago Brave bears dark red self flowers over a clean green throat, blooming in midseason with reliable rebloom on scapes about 28 inches tall. Introduced in 1976, it belongs to the same lineage of 'Chicago'-prefixed cultivars that became a hallmark of mid-twentieth-century daylily breeding, and it earned an American Hemerocallis Society Honorable Mention. The semi-evergreen foliage performs well across a wide range of climates. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Olive Bailey Langdon Daylily (Purple Self with Yellow-Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Olive Bailey Langdon is a 1974 tetraploid bred from Embassy crossed with Chicago Regal, both long-established garden cultivars.

directions: Olive Bailey Langdon bears soothing purple-orchid self flowers about five inches across with a contrasting yellow-green throat, opening early-to-midseason with dependable rebloom on scapes roughly 28 inches tall. This semi-evergreen tetraploid was bred in 1974 from a cross of 'Embassy' and 'Chicago Regal', and it went on to collect multiple American Hemerocallis Society honors over the following decade, a testament to its enduring garden performance. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain heavy flowering.

common_name: Green Widow Daylily (Yellow-Green Spider with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Widow is a 1980 spider-form daylily later used as a parent of 'Banana Pepper Spider'.

directions: Green Widow is a true spider-form daylily bearing unusually narrow, long-petaled, yellow-green flowers about seven inches across above a matching green throat, held on wiry scapes roughly two feet tall. Registered in 1980, this evergreen diploid later won the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award for best spider and was used as a parent of the later spider introduction 'Banana Pepper Spider'. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to keep bloom counts high.

common_name: Thin Man Daylily (Unusual-Form Red Self with Yellow-Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Thin Man is a 2002 introduction with an unusual-form flower and strong rebloom.

directions: Thin Man bears bright red self flowers above a yellow-green throat, classified by the American Hemerocallis Society as an unusual-form cultivar for its distinctively narrow, elongated petals, opening on tall scapes around 42 inches through a midseason display with reliable rebloom. Introduced in 2002, it has since earned AHS honors including an Award of Merit and the Lambert/Webster Award. This evergreen tetraploid is easy to grow in average garden soil; divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Catherine Neal Daylily (Late-Season Purple Self with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Catherine Neal is a 1981 introduction valued for its unusually late bloom window and reliable rebloom.

directions: Catherine Neal bears purple self flowers about six inches across over a clean green throat, opening very late in the daylily season on scapes roughly 30 inches tall and reblooming once established. Introduced in 1981, this dormant diploid extends the bloom calendar well past most midseason cultivars, making it useful for gardeners wanting color after earlier daylilies have finished. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
